messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

As a chaplain at a busy hospital, 44-year-old Maya had always been drawn to helping others in their darkest moments. But after surviving a terrorist attack on a crowded train three years ago, she found herself struggling to cope with the aftermath. The traumatic event still felt like yesterday - the smell of smoke and sweat, the sound of screams and shattering glass, the sight of chaos and destruction. When Maya thinks back to that day, it's not just the memories that flood her mind but also a sense of disorientation and confusion. She can't quite put the events in order, and the sensory details feel more vivid than any ordinary memory (Confused Sequence, More Real Than Normal). As she relives those moments, Maya is convinced that she should have done something to prevent it - if only she had been more vigilant or proactive (Bad Coper). Maya's fear of losing control and being at the mercy of events has become an all-consuming concern. She can't bear to be in situations where she feels trapped or helpless, like when people misbehave or authority figures try to exert their power over her (Loss of Control, Avoid Authority Figures). Even positive emotions, like joy or excitement, feel tainted by the memory of that day - as if happiness is a luxury she can no longer afford (Positive Emotion Confusion). In an attempt to regain some sense of control, Maya has developed a range of coping strategies. She performs mental rituals to ward off bad thoughts and prevent another disaster from happening (Magical Prevention). She also restricts her food intake, as if by controlling what goes into her body, she can somehow shield herself from the world's dangers (Undereating). Maya's perceptions of the world have become increasingly distorted. She believes that institutions failed to protect her - if only they had been more vigilant or proactive, the attack might have been prevented (Institutional Failure). As a result, she has lost trust in authority figures and feels like she's on her own in navigating the dangers of life. As Maya navigates her daily environment, she is constantly on high alert. She chooses where to sit based on how safe or protected she feels (Safe Seat Seeking), watches others closely for signs that they might harm her (Watching Others), and is startled by unexpected sounds (Threat in Sounds). Her memories of the event seem to be triggered by these environmental cues, sending her spiraling back into a world of fear and anxiety. Maya's maladaptive strategies have become self-reinforcing. By restricting her food intake or performing mental rituals, she feels like she's taking control - but this only serves to heighten her sense of threat and reinforce her negative appraisals (Maladaptive Strategies → Threat). Her memories of the event continue to haunt her, fueling her fear that the world is a dangerous place (Memory → Negative Appraisals). Despite her best efforts, Maya can't shake off the feeling that she's living on borrowed time. She's started to question whether she's cut out for this line of work - or indeed, whether she's capable of coping with life at all. As she struggles to reconcile her faith with the trauma she's experienced, Maya has come to realize that she needs help - not just to heal from her physical wounds but also to repair the emotional and psychological damage that still lingers. It was this growing awareness of her own limitations and vulnerabilities that finally brought Maya to seek professional help. She hopes that therapy will allow her to process her memories and emotions in a healthier way, and perhaps even learn to trust herself - and others - once again. But for now, the fear and anxiety remain, a constant reminder of the trauma she's endured and the long road ahead.
